div.head: Norðleoda Inscr.
div.ab: The law of the North-people. (Of wergild[s, Ld] hlq).
The law of the North people (Norðleoda laga)
div.note: Liebermann prints D (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College 201, p. 102, after Geþyncðo, c. 1060), H (Textus Roffensis f. 93v, after Geþyncðo, c. 1120) and Ld (Lambarde's print), with the Quadripartitus. K is H; D is also given here. H's heading is in red. ‘Nordleute’ are the Anglo-Scandinavians of northern England. Liebermann dates the core c. 920–954; the language of the archetype and the compilation need only date from c. 1050; the compiler perhaps also wrote or knew Geþyncðo and Mirce, and was perhaps a Mercian. ‘hlq’ is the exemplar of H and lq (lq = exemplar of Ld and the Quadripartitus). Clause number standardised from ‘Norðleod Inscr.’.; AA: corrected against Rabin p. 12, October 2026 (was “Concerning”, now “On”); AT: added from Whitelock p. 477, October 2026 (Whitelock’s footnotes); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date in the running heads), October 2026 (was “1002–23 (Whitelock); 1006–8 (Rabin)”, now “c.920–954 (Liebermann); 1002–23 (Whitelock); 1006–8 (Rabin)”); F: corrected against Liebermann, Gesetze I (date at the head of the text); Wormald, Making of English Law I; Whitelock, English Historical Documents I, October 2026 (was “c.920–954 (Liebermann); 1002–23 (Whitelock); 1006–8 (Rabin)”, now “c.920–954 (Liebermann, I p. 458); 1002–23 (Whitelock, EHD p. 475); 1006–8 (Rabin)”); BQ: page of each of Liebermann’s texts and of his German, checked against Liebermann, Gesetze I (our double-read transcription), October 2026 (e.g. was “(empty)”, now “D 458; H 458; Ld 458; German 459”; 14 rows of Norðleoda)

note.seg: das frühe Datum trifft nur den inhaltlichen Kern der Arbeit; die Sprache des Archetyps und die Compilation brauchen erst etwa 1050 entstanden zu sein. Der Compilator verfasste oder kannte oder beeinflusste auch Geþyncðo und Mirce; er war vielleicht Mercier, laut 6; Að Inscr.

the early date applies only to the substantive core of the work; the language of the archetype and the compilation need not have arisen until about 1050. The compiler also composed or knew or influenced Geþyncðo and Mirce; he was perhaps a Mercian, according to 6; Að Inscr.

note.seg: Die Überschrift, sowohl die in D wie die in hlq, kann dem folgenden Text bloss entnommen sein. Möglicherweise jedoch ist eine davon archetyp. Dagegen die in Q n gehört erst dem Rubrikator 1115—40; s. o. S. 247 Rect Insc¹

The heading, both that in D and that in hlq, may simply have been taken from the following text. Possibly, however, one of them is archetypal. The one in Q n, by contrast, belongs only to the rubricator of 1115—40; see above p. 247 Rect Insc¹

Vgl. Gl Norðleod 1; Denalagu 1d-g; Tollers Übs. ‘northfolk of England, Angles’ ist zu allgemein, untechnisch. Im 10. Jh. bildeten nämlich die Angeln weder Einen Staat noch wurden sie als Ganzes national unterschieden. Synonym steht (neben and. Bedd.) norðerne men (~folc), Norð(an)hymbre (sbst., adj.: ~ lcod), Norðengle, -men, -folc. ‘Norfolk’ im heutigen Sinne, woran Schmid S. lxv dachte, kommt erst seit 11. Jh. vor; der Erzbischof würde dort nicht passen; und es war nie ein Königreich

Cf. Gl Norðleod 1; Denalagu 1d-g; Toller’s translation ‘northfolk of England, Angles’ is too general and untechnical. For in the 10th cent. the Angles neither formed a single state nor were they distinguished nationally as a whole. Synonymous (besides other meanings) are norðerne men (~folc), Norð(an)hymbre (noun, adj.: ~ lcod), Norðengle, -men, -folc. ‘Norfolk’ in the present-day sense, which Schmid p. lxv had in mind, occurs only from the 11th cent.; the archbishop would not fit there; and it was never a kingdom
lq = Vorlage von Ld und Quadr.; hlq = Vorlage von H und lq
lq = exemplar of Ld and Quadr.; hlq = exemplar of H and lq

The texts I include under this heading are those called by Liebermann Geþyncðo, Norðleoda laga, Mircna laga. Að and Hadbot, and printed by him, I, 456–69. Thorpe has the three first, in a different order, I, 186–93. The five texts occur in C.C.C.C., MS. 201, a manuscript with connections with Archbishop Wulfstan, and D.Bethurum has produced good reasons for assigning the collection to this prelate, who was deeply interested in this matter. The last three are also in C.C.C.C.. MS. 190, another manuscript connected with Wulfstan. All five, but not as a group or in order, are in the Textus Roffensis, and the authors of Quadripartitus and the Instituta Cnuti use them. Much of what is known of status in Anglo-Saxon times comes from these texts, which should not be regarded as official enactments but as a private compilation. [Her footnote 2: No. 52 in the 1955 edition] [Her footnote 3: Journ. Engl. and Germ. Phil., xlix, 449–63]
